clippings.sign: FISH SURVEYED ON SEATING; NO REPLIES YET
clippings.refuse: FISH NOT CONSULTED; ANGLERS SIT WHERE THEY SAT

afterSign.text: Rodney proposes pressing your one bar as a record. Both sides.
afterSign.subject: vanity

clippings.sign: GOVERNOR'S ONE BAR RELEASED; REVIEWS BRIEF
clippings.refuse: ONE BAR REMAINS ONE BAR

afterRefuse.text: The band kept your bar. Conduct half of it? Less to go wrong.
afterRefuse.subject: bandstands

clippings.sign: GOVERNOR CONDUCTS HALF A BAR; BAND FINISHES IT
clippings.refuse: BAR STILL UNCONDUCTED; BAND PLAYS IT ANYWAY

afterSign.text: Our tuba thrives alone. Each cornet now wants a shelter, by the canal.
afterSign.subject: bandstands

clippings.sign: GOVERNOR CUTS RIBBON ON SHELTER FOR ONE CORNET
clippings.refuse: CORNETS SHARE A SHELTER; NOBODY SPEAKS

afterRefuse.text: Our tuba asks for shop doorways instead. It rattles only 1 pane in 3.
afterRefuse.subject: bandstands

clippings.sign: TUBA IN THE DOORWAYS; WINDOWS ON EDGE

applications.text: I apply to be Minister for Potholes. References: 'She found one.'
applications.returnText: I apply again. Since last time, I have found another one.

applications.text: I apply to be Minister for Benches. I ended the onion dispute. Both onions now speak.
applications.returnText: I apply again. The onions asked after you.

applications.text: I apply to be Minister for Lampposts. I once found a sponsor for a puddle.
applications.returnText: I apply again. The puddle still speaks well of me.

applications.text: I apply to be Minister for Market Weights. Rumours lose interest when I walk in.
applications.returnText: I apply again. Nobody mentioned I had gone.

applications.text: Minister for Bandstands, please. 212 ribbon-cuttings; I know when the scissors close.
applications.returnText: I apply again. I have kept the fanfare warm.

applications.text: I apply to be Minister for Jetties. I can open a fête with a third of the fuss.
applications.returnText: I apply again. The chair is already unfolded.

applications.text: Minister for Kites, please. I once kept a kite up for nine hours. I was asked for one.
applications.returnText: I apply again. The kite is still up.

applications.text: I apply to run the Hedgerow Bureau. I have said nothing, very well, for thirty years.
applications.returnText: I apply again. I did not mention it to anyone.

applications.text: I apply for Jetties. I have patched the same waders for twenty years. They are all patch.
applications.returnText: I apply again. In the same waders.

grievances.text: No more pumpkins until you return our ribbon scissors. You know which scissors.

grievances.text: You posed with our bus stop and kept it. We now wait at a lamp post.
grievances.subject: buses

grievances.text: No displays until our mirror is back. You were only going to check your hat.
grievances.subject: vanity

grievances.text: No practice until our room is back. Your portrait sitting is in its sixth week.
grievances.subject: portraits

grievances.text: No buses logged until our logbook is back. You signed every page, then the cover.
grievances.subject: buses

grievances.text: Bare windows until the hat from window four is back. It suited the stand better.
grievances.subject: hats

grievances.text: No sitting until our QUIET PLEASE sign is back. You held it up at your speech.
grievances.subject: signage

grievances.text: No weigh-in until our first-prize rosette is back. You did not enter.
grievances.subject: vegetable-shows

grievances.text: Our best kite was lent for a photograph. It is now framed in your hall.
grievances.subject: kites

grievances.text: No concerts until our music stands come back. They are holding up your portraits.
grievances.subject: portraits

grievances.text: Our show hedge went behind you in a photograph. It has not come back.
grievances.subject: hedges

grievances.text: No trimming until our spirit level is back. Your nameplate is straight now.
grievances.subject: hedges

grievances.text: No launches until our string is back. You keep cutting it at openings.
grievances.subject: ribbons

grievances.text: We will not sit until the pond gets its name back. It never asked for yours.
grievances.subject: vanity

frontPages.text: MAYOR HOLDS OPENING FOR NEW SCISSORS. Old scissors not invited.

frontPages.subject: vanity

frontPages.subject: vanity

frontPages.text: GOVERNOR UNVEILS PLAQUE TO UNVEILING OF PLAQUE. Another planned.
frontPages.subject: ceremonies

frontPages.text: GOVERNOR REOPENS FOOTBRIDGE FOR THIRD TIME. It had never closed.
frontPages.subject: ceremonies

frontPages.text: GOVERNOR CUTS ONE RIBBON NINE TIMES FOR CAMERAS. Ribbon now confetti.
frontPages.subject: ribbons

frontPages.text: GOVERNOR POSES WITH PHOTOGRAPH OF GOVERNOR. Both 'looking well'.
frontPages.subject: portraits

frontPages.text: GOVERNOR FILLS IN FORM REQUESTING OWN AUTOGRAPH. Request granted.

frontPages.text: PRESIDENT'S SIGNATURE GIVEN ITS OWN DESK. Law signed on the floor.

frontPages.text: PRESIDENT REHEARSES OWN SURPRISE BIRTHDAY. 'Very convincing'.
frontPages.subject: vanity

frontPages.text: PRESIDENT'S CAKE GETS PRESS OFFICER. Cake 'not taking questions'.
frontPages.subject: vanity

frontPages.text: PRESIDENT NAMES CLOUD AFTER SELF. Cloud moves on.

frontPages.text: PRESIDENT'S NAME ADDED TO DICTIONARY. Defined as 'see ribbon'.
frontPages.subject: ribbons

frontPages.text: PRESIDENT PRACTISES HANDSHAKE ON DOOR. Door 'warmly received'.
frontPages.subject: ceremonies

frontPages.text: PRESIDENT HAS CARPET ROLLED OUT TO KETTLE. Tea takes an hour.

runUp.text: Judge the {district} Prize Hedge Show. Say nothing about the leaning one.

runUp.text: Award {district}'s best-kept bench. Do not sit on it. It is kept.

runUp.subject: vanity

runUp.text: Lean on the {district} gate, thoughtfully. The gate is on loan.
runUp.subject: vanity

runUp.text: Unveil a plaque in {district}, where you once unveiled a plaque.

runUp.text: Plant a tree in {district}. It will be photogenic in 40 years.

runUp.text: Pin the {district} show rosette on the winner. Not on you.

runUp.text: Award the {district} prizes: best scone, best rose, best photo of you.

runUp.text: Sign the {district} visitors' book. Not the napkin; that is the law.
runUp.subject: paperwork

runUp.text: Sit by the water in {district}. Say nothing. You will be quoted.

runUp.text: Tour {district}: 14 benches, and not one has your name. Yet.
runUp.subject: vanity

runUp.text: Break new ground in {district}. Gently; it is the bowling green.

runUp.text: Hand over the {district} band cup. We play you on. Off. And on.

runUp.text: Pose with the {district} prize pumpkin. It has been told where to look.

runUp.text: Hold the {district} ribbon. Someone else cuts it. Smile anyway.

runUp.text: Present the {district} cup. It reads: THE PRESIDENT, AND THE WINNER.

runUp.text: Inspect the {district} fishing pegs. Nod. Nodding has a form.

runUp.text: Sit for the {district} art club. They asked for a bowl of fruit.

runUp.text: Read the {district} timetable aloud. All of it. Mervyn checks.

runUp.text: Sniff every rose at the {district} rose show. All 400. Look delighted.

runUp.text: Ring the {district} bell once. Then once for the photograph.

night.text: Stitchley: I still own the hat.
Dunnock: Nobody is home, then. Understood.
Setter: Defeated. Eight letters. I checked.
Waft: The spoon will be disappointed. I shall tell it gently.
Mallowby: I shall play something short on the way out. In a minor key.
Noonday: It was never my hour. It has clouded over anyway.
Kalends: I have crossed out today. It will not be missed.
Strop: I shall remain seated. Thank you.
Ringrose: The handbells would like to congratulate you. One at a time.
Mould: Nothing is wasted. I shall put this evening on the heap.
Dovecote: I shall send word. By the usual route.
Pharos: I shall leave a small light on for you.
Lathe: I shall add this evening to the tapestry. A small corner.
Furlong: A short tune for the winner. Very short.
Tessel: There is always one piece missing. I will look under the table.
Pantry: Unsettled, then. I shall take my coat.
Ambling: I shall walk home. The scenic way.
Knapp: I shall congratulate you properly. Please stand well back.
Good evening. I will read each envelope once. Applause after, please.
Good evening. I have a new stick of chalk, and a spare.
Held. One rosette, pinned straight.
Held. For the back of the room: held.
Not held. I will chalk it neatly, all the same.
To your opponent. The rosette goes back in its box.
That is a majority. The band may begin.
That is a majority. Please do not cut anything yet.
That is a majority for your opponent. I will read the rest, as is proper.
Your opponent has a majority. The band will play something quieter.
Quiet at the back, please. Thank you.
A reminder: the tea urn is off during the reading.

returning.text: The same paper as before. It has been ironed.
The same paper. The visitor hopes you have changed instead.
Back again. Cuthbert has filed it under AGAIN.
This paper has been here before. This time it wiped its feet.
Back again. Rodney advises you to look as if you remember it.
The same request, now with a covering letter about the request.
Back again. They say it is a different paper. It is the same paper.
Word for word as before. They practised on the stairs.
Back again. Gwendolyn has the old answer ready, if you want to save time.
Here once more, with the same words, said more slowly.
A fresh envelope. The words inside are not fresh.
Back again. They have brought their own chair.
Back again. They now know everyone in the corridor by name.
The request is the same. The handwriting is neater.
Returned, unchanged, with a note pinned on: STILL ASKING.
Back again, by appointment. They made the appointment.
They have heard you like ribbons. There is one round it now.
Back again. It says it was in the area.
Back again, at exactly the same time as last time.
Back again. You have been spotted, and it is in the notebook.
Back again, with the same paper and fresh sandwiches. They expect a wait.
Back again. Your office is now a request stop in their notebook.
Back again. There is a footnote now, and it has a footnote.
Back again, with the timetable of their next visit attached.
Back again. The paper has spent the week in a shop window.
Back again. They have looked at your office window and have notes.
Back again. The paper has been dressed for the season.
Back again, in a frame, lit from below.
Back again. They rang the bell at your door. Your door has no bell.
Returned in tissue paper, with a bow tied at a careful angle.
Back again, with the same pumpkin and a firmer tone.
The paper has been entered for a rosette. It was highly commended.
Back again. It has been turned once a day, so it ripens evenly.
Back again. They have weighed the paper, for fairness.
Back again. They brought the paper in a wheelbarrow, out of habit.
Back again. It has been kept in a cool, dry place, as the label says.
Back again, humming the request under their breath.
The request has since been arranged for full band.
The same request, now with a second verse.
Back again. The paper now has its own music stand.
A cornet waits in the corridor, in case your answer needs a fanfare.
The paper is back, written a little louder.
Back again, so quietly you almost missed it.
The paper came back under the door without a sound.
Back again. They have sat in the corridor since dawn, perfectly still.
Back again. They have not said a word. They are waiting for a bite.
They waited by the water cooler, as if it were a pond.
Back again. They ask that you sign or study it quietly.
Back again. They looked up at your ceiling first, out of habit.
The paper has a tail on it now, for steadiness.
Back again. They have opened your window, just in case.
The paper arrived slightly before they did.
Back again, folded into something that very nearly flies.
Back again. They have let out a little more string.
Back again. They have seen your office plant and are not mentioning it.
Back again. The margins have been measured, twice.
Your pens are now in a straight line. They did that while waiting.
Back again, with shears, in case the paper needs editing.
The paper has been clipped since. Only the parts that stuck out.
Back again. They have checked that your desk is level. It is not.

away.text: The clock chimed the hours without you. It managed.
Cuthbert put the stationery cupboard in order, then the stationery.
Gwendolyn balanced the books, then, to pass the time, balanced them again.
Rodney told the newspaper you were working very hard elsewhere.
Your desk wore a sign saying BACK SHORTLY. It has been very patient.
The ministries collected without you. Gwendolyn says they barely noticed.
Rodney wrote a speech for your return. It is mostly about you.
A committee watered the office plant, after a short meeting.
Your photograph kept an eye on things. It has nothing to report.
Your chair was kept warm by a cushion with your name on it.

captions.text: Mayor of Dithering-on-the-Dawdle, unopposed. The other candidate went to the wrong hall.
Governor of Upper Wobbling. A mahogany desk, a green lamp, and Pruella, near lunch.
President. A walnut desk, three telephones, and Mildred, who liked one of the last three.
The winner resigned for a hobby. You serve on, as Acting. Rodney had it painted small.
Every district held. Rodney is having the result framed, and then the frame.

monuments.name: A bust of yourself
monuments.text: In bronze, facing the door, so that visitors meet you twice.

monuments.name: A bust of the bust
monuments.text: The first bust looked lonely. This one gazes at it, admiringly.

monuments.name: Bronze ribbon scissors
monuments.text: They can no longer cut anything. You still bring them to openings.

monuments.name: A ribbon, cut, in bronze
monuments.text: Cut by you, then cast in bronze. It cannot be cut again, which you regret.

monuments.name: Your parking space, in bronze
monuments.text: Nobody may park on it now. You park beside it and visit.

monuments.name: A hat with a smaller hat on it
monuments.text: Cast from Tobias Slake's gift. He has since sent a smaller hat, for the top.

monuments.name: The prize pumpkin, in bronze
monuments.text: Cast from the prize pumpkin itself, which sat very still for it.

monuments.name: A bench with your name
monuments.text: Your name runs along the backrest in raised letters. Visitors leave wearing it.

monuments.name: A plaque to the plaque
monuments.text: It marks the unveiling of the first plaque. A third will mark this one.

monuments.name: Your first pen
monuments.text: The pen that signed your first paper. You had not read that one either.

monuments.name: The in-tray, empty at last
monuments.text: Cast on the one afternoon it was empty. There is a photograph.

monuments.name: A committee of three chairs
monuments.text: Three bronze chairs face each other. They have not yet decided.

monuments.name: A fountain shaped like you
monuments.text: Lavinia Plash calls it a perfect likeness. It, too, never stops talking.

monuments.name: Your umbrella, in bronze
monuments.text: Crispin Mizzle's gift, cast so that it can never be lost. Nor opened.

monuments.name: A pothole, preserved
monuments.text: The oldest pothole there is, behind a rope. You opened it to the public.

monuments.name: A handshake with yourself
monuments.text: Both hands are yours. Both look delighted to meet you.

monuments.name: The most adequate trophy
monuments.text: Awarded to you, by you, for adequacy. The engraving is adequate.

monuments.name: A sundial set by you
monuments.text: It tells the time by your arrival, so you have never once been late.

monuments.name: A bandstand for one
monuments.text: There is room for you and a music stand. The band sends its regards.

monuments.name: A kite that will not fly
monuments.text: Bronze, string and all. It was flown once, by crane, for the photograph.

monuments.name: A teapot that chimes
monuments.text: A gift from Till's Teas. It chimes on the hour and pours on the half.

monuments.name: A duck, unveiled
monuments.text: The duck you once fed, on camera. It came to the unveiling, briefly.

monuments.name: A rosette of rosettes
monuments.text: Every rosette you ever pinned on yourself, sewn into one. All first prize.

monuments.name: You, pointing at something
monuments.text: A statue of you, pointing at something important. It is the bus station.

store.subtitle: Sign silly papers, run a town
store.shortDescription: Pull a paper down to refuse it, push it up to sign. A comedy of town office.
store.description:
An invented country and a comedy desk: pull a paper down into the drawer marked FOR FURTHER STUDY, or push it up to sign it.

You are the new mayor of Dithering-on-the-Dawdle, in the Republic of Middling (motto: Proudly Adequate). You were elected unopposed. The other candidate went to the wrong hall.

Visitors queue at your door. A bus spotter would like the 7:02 named after you. A pumpkin grower asks for the freedom of the town for her pumpkin, which has asked very politely. A lobbyist leaves a small fruit basket, for no reason. Each paper prints both outcomes before you touch it, in exact numbers: what signing costs or pays, which club it pleases and which it annoys, and whether the poll moves. Those are the numbers applied. A signed paper rests on the out-tray for two seconds; tap it to take it back.

The town's opinion belongs to its hobby clubs: the Bus Spotters' Society, the Shop Window Guild and the Giant Vegetable Society, with a brass band, anglers, kite flyers and a hedge committee further up. Their approval multiplies everything your ministries earn, from x0.4 at 0 % to x1.6 at 100 %. A club pushed too far boycotts its ministry until you settle with it or 8 more papers are decided. Let the gossip pile up and the town paper prints a front page about you: apologise on the steps, or say nothing and collect a fifth less for 10 papers.

A term is a fixed number of papers. Late in the term you may call the election. The poll board shows exactly how each ward would vote today, and on election night a clerk chalks up the wards, safest first. Win, and your Name Recognition grows; with enough of it, and a record of ministry levels to match, you may stand for Governor of Upper Wobbling, then President in Middlingham, taking your ministers with you. Lose, and nothing you built is lost: you carry on as Acting Mayor, and the winner resigns to spend more time with her hat.

Taxes, at least, need no signature, which makes this technically an idle game. Four ministries in town (six as Governor, eight as President) collect dibs every second. With the app shut they go on collecting at 35 % of the rate, for a maximum of 4 hours, and a visitor leaves a paper every 6 minutes, until 10 wait in the in-tray. Moods, gossip, the poll and the term wait for you to read.

At the desk a visitor comes about every 12 seconds. When nobody is waiting, the Treasury Clerk slides a budget slip across, and a flick up buys what she advises: a level or a new ministry. Nine ministers apply for posts along the way; each runs one ministry and brings one desk rule, printed on every paper it touches. The levels go into the Ledger, a clothbound book kept for the tycoon in you.

Everything here is invented: the country, its towns and clubs, its politicians, companies and newspapers. There are no parties, and nobody can type a name into the game.

Watching an ad is always your choice, made from a button that names its reward: half again on the away report; Check the Sofa, a small sum once a term; Call the Spin Doctor, which ends the cost of saying nothing; Send a Courier, which ends a boycott; Open the Doors, which fills the in-tray. No banners appear, and no ad plays between screens. Five purchases, none of them random: Junior Clerk on Duty (the Standing Order from your first day: the junior clerk buys the advised ministry level while you play), Long Lunch (time away counts for 6 hours, not 4), the Walnut & Brass Desk Set and Gilt Portrait Frames (both looks only), and Skip the Ad Videos: your secretary sits through them, and the reward arrives at once. From the moment you call an election until election night ends, no ad or purchase is offered. No ad or purchase moves a mood or a poll point: those move only by papers you decide.
store.promotionalText: The Republic of Middling needs a mayor who reads. You will do. Grant a pumpkin the freedom of the town, decline a fruit basket, call the election when the poll is kind.
